final_response:
\boxed{\text{Let }C=2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac1{k^a}\text{ (finite since }a>1\text{). Set }x_0=0\text{, and inductively pick }x_n\in[0,C]\text{ such that }|x_n-x_j|\ge (n-j)^{-a}\text{ for all }j<n.}

**Derivation.** At step $n$, the values forbidden for $x_n$ lie in $\bigcup_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl(x_j-\frac1{(n-j)^a},\,x_j+\frac1{(n-j)^a}\bigr)$. The total length of this union intersected with $[0,C]$ is at most $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{2}{(n-j)^a}=2\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1{k^a}<C$. Hence the union cannot cover $[0,C]$, so a valid choice of $x_n$ exists. By construction $|x_i-x_j|\ge|i-j|^{-a}$ for every $i\ne j$, i.e. $|x_i-x_j||i-j|^a\ge1$, and all terms satisfy $|x_n|\le C$, so the sequence is bounded.
